demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one', the body-focused appraisals 'I can no longer trust my own body' and 'I feel ashamed of what happened to my body' are hard to reconcile clinically unless the patient also directly experienced major bodily violation/injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

The memory items imply vivid sensory reliving of the traumatic event ('hear things ... heard during the frightening event') and fragmented visual snapshots, which can occur in PTSD, but here they are not well matched to the selected appraisals: the profile centers on bodily shame/unreliability rather than grief/death-related meanings of the event.

'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly integrated: there are no trigger or threat items tying work contexts to the trauma, and the formulation does not include trigger/threat pathways. The coping profile otherwise concerns sleep delay and undereating, so work avoidance feels insufficiently anchored.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, body-focused shame is clinically hard to reconcile unless there was also direct bodily violation, injury, or assault. The rest of the profile centers grief-related loss, meaning, and intrusive memory phenomena, so this item appears inconsistent with the trauma type and with the other selected items.

vignette:
Malia is a forty-six-year-old forensic analyst who, eighteen months ago, received a phone call that changed everything. Her younger brother, a healthy and active man of thirty-eight, had collapsed at a community gathering and died before paramedics could revive him. She was not there. The call came from her mother, and what she remembers most vividly is not the words but the sound—the raw, animal quality of her mother's voice breaking, a sound that now plays in her head without warning. When the memory returns, it arrives not as a full story but as a series of frozen snapshots: the phone in her hand, the kitchen clock reading 9:47 PM, the pattern on the linoleum floor. Each image is so sharp and so overwhelming that she has to stop whatever she is doing—once, in the middle of an evidence review, she dropped her tablet and sat at her desk with her hands over her ears, unable to speak to the colleague who asked if she was all right.

Her work as a forensic analyst had once given her a clear sense of purpose. She analyzed crime scene data, pieced together timelines, and believed that every detail held meaning. Now the lab feels like a place where nothing matters. She has lost faith in the order she once trusted—if her brother could die without warning, then the careful logic of her work is just a thin layer over chaos. She has stopped volunteering for case reviews and avoids the sections of the database that contain autopsy photos or 911 recordings, though she never said why to her supervisor. Instead she calls in sick more often, or sits in her car in the parking lot until the last possible moment. When she does go inside, she stays late at her desk after everyone leaves, not because she is productive but because she cannot bear to go home and lie in the dark. She delays sleep until two or three in the morning, watching mindless videos or scrolling social media, anything to avoid the moment when her mind is quiet and the snapshots might return. Her appetite has dwindled to nearly nothing; she eats a piece of toast in the morning and forgets to eat again until her husband reminds her, and even then the food tastes like cardboard.

Her husband, a high school teacher, has grown quiet and careful around her. He stopped asking about her day weeks ago, because every attempt ends in silence or tears. Malia knows he is worried, but she cannot explain what she feels because she barely understands it herself. She has come to believe that her life, the one she had before the phone call, has been destroyed. The forensic data she once found fascinating now seems hollow—what difference does it make who left a fingerprint, when death can come so arbitrarily? She has lost all sense of meaning. Religion had never been central to her, but she used to feel a kind of secular faith in human decency; now she sees strangers on the street and thinks only of how fragile they are, how easily gone.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago. She was listening to a recorded interview for a case—routine, no death involved—and the sound of the interviewee's voice cracking on a syllable triggered a full recall of her mother's call. She froze in her cubicle, heart pounding, and could not move for several minutes. Her supervisor found her and suggested, with gentle concern, that she take some time off. Malia agreed, but she was more afraid of what would happen if she stopped working entirely—her job was the last structure she had. She scheduled an appointment with a psychologist because she is terrified that she is losing herself, that the broken sound in her head will never fade, and that the meaning she once found in her work and her family is gone for good. She does not know if she can get it back, but she knows she cannot keep going the way she is.
